entries.finding: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomized studies found cranberry consumption significantly reduced BMI, while pooled body weight and waist circumference effects were not significant.
The 2026 cranberry review found the BMI reduction was also observed in subgroup analyses among adults over 50, overweight participants, and interventions lasting more than eight weeks.
The 2026 cranberry meta-analysis found no significant overall effects on AST, ALT, or alkaline phosphatase, so the pooled evidence did not support a generalized liver-enzyme benefit.
Although overall AST was not significantly changed, the 2026 review reported an increase in AST within certain BMI-reduction subgroups, adding an important safety and interpretation boundary.

A 2026 systematic review covering 50 randomized trials found fenugreek-derived preparations consistently improved glycemic outcomes across the included metabolic-health studies, although substantial heterogeneity remained.
The 2026 fenugreek systematic review found guar gum produced more consistent lipid effects than fenugreek, illustrating that metabolic effects differed by galactomannan source.
Effects of fenugreek-derived preparations on body weight and BMI were less consistent than their glycemic findings in the 2026 systematic review.
The 2026 review included fenugreek seed powder, seed extract, and leaf extract studies, with differences in participants, dose, and treatment duration contributing to substantial heterogeneity.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials involving 802 participants found Syzygium cumini and related Myrtaceae interventions produced a statistically significant but modest reduction in fasting plasma glucose, with very high heterogeneity.

The 2026 Syzygium cumini review described the clinical evidence as fragmented and heterogeneous, so the pooled fasting-glucose signal should not be treated as proof of a standardized effect across preparations.

The 2026 review specifically evaluated efficacy and safety of Syzygium cumini and related Myrtaceae interventions, reflecting that safety evidence is part of the clinical evidence base rather than an assumed property of the plant.

A 2025 network meta-analysis of 18 randomized trials involving 2,177 breast-cancer patients found silymarin from milk thistle was associated with lower risk of grade 2-or-higher radiation dermatitis versus standard care in the included evidence network.

The same 2025 network meta-analysis found no plant-derived intervention demonstrated superiority over standard care for preventing grade 3-or-higher radiation dermatitis, limiting extrapolation of the silymarin finding to severe dermatitis.
